ann_115.text: Through this part, capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% at none to about 9% at 6849 US dollars, for most people slowly at first, then faster, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower; but for people not living in a family it stays flat at first, then falls steadily.

For most people they lower it slowly at first, then faster once they rise above about 3912 US dollars, but for people not living in a family it stays flat at first, then falls steadily: for the typical person, going from 0 to 5013 US dollars clearly lowers it from about 55% to about 40%, and 2300 of the 39073 training people are already past that point.
The drop is clearly larger for people who do not live in a family, from about 69% to about 10%, against about 55% to about 9% for others.
Not living in a family by itself clearly lowers it through this part, from about 55% to about 39%.

ann_116.text: Through this part, being older clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily up to about 38 years, then no further: from about 84% at 22 years to about 50% at 58 years.

ann_117.text: Through this part, being born outside the United States raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to about 63% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 3950 people were born outside the United States.

ann_118.text: Through this part, being born in Scotland raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to above 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
Only 16 people in the training data were born in Scotland.

ann_119.text: Through this part, being another relative in the household lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to about 47% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 1180 people are other relatives in the household.

ann_120.text: Through this part, being born in El Salvador slightly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 55% to about 58%.
In the training data, 119 people were born in El Salvador.

ann_121.text: This part acts on 37903 of 39073 training people, and 28889 of them have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical person it acts on (the same 37-year-old married man), it slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 51% to about 55%.
Through it, handling or cleaning work clearly raises the typical person's predicted chance from about 55% to about 73%.
That rise is clearly smaller for Asian or Pacific Islander people (from about 57% to about 72%) than for others (to about 79%).
Being Asian or Pacific Islander by itself slightly lowers it, from about 55% to about 51% (on the training data only).

ann_122.text: Through this part, federal government work lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to about 42% (on the training data only).

It acts on the 1132 federal employees among 39073 training people, 686 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical one (a 43-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in an administrative or clerical job, working 40 hours a week), it lowers the predicted chance from about 59% to about 46% (on the training data only).

ann_123.text: Through this part, transport or moving work slightly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 55% to about 58%.
In the training data, 1934 people work in transport or moving.

ann_124.text: Through this part, being unmarried clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to about 47%.

It acts on the 4059 unmarried people among 39073 training people, 3820 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; for the typical person it acts on (a 39-year-old White divorced woman born in the United States, unmarried, a high-school graduate at level 9 on the 1-16 scale in an administrative or clerical job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it slightly lowers the predicted chance, staying at about 98%.

ann_125.text: Through this part, a missing country of birth or being married with the spouse absent slightly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, to about 53% and 54% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 677 people have a missing country of birth and 487 are married with the spouse absent.

ann_126.text: Through this part, a higher education level and capital losses both clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: from about 78% at 7 to about 31% at 13 on the 1-16 education scale, and from about 55% at no capital losses to about 27% at 1887 US dollars.
Not being married, farming or fishing, being neither husband nor wife and other service work clearly raise it to about 81% to 83%, missing occupation to about 78%, and being a woman to about 72%.
